candidate: Guard rules for trust-handoff and control-plane paths (kit-native, no version)
what: Deny agent writes to files that a trusted tool later runs or obeys, and to the kit's own control files, on every platform; after each unattended run list protected files whose hashes changed.
problem_here: The guard seals data and freezes evaluator paths but does not cover git hooks, git config, shell startup files, editor and agent configuration, MCP configuration, rule files, or the kit's own config, budgets and ledger. On native Windows there is no sandbox to cover them either.
mechanism: Extra deny patterns in nn_guard.py for Write, Edit and shell redirection into .git/hooks, .git/config, .gitmodules, shell startup files, .vscode, .idea, .claude, .codex, .cursor, .mcp.json, agent rule files and the kit's state directory; expctl hash extended to these paths and compared before and after a run.
evidence: 61 of 79 measured sandbox escapes broke no configured rule and 37 were trust handoff (https://carlostapia.cl/notes/sandbox-escapes-no-rule-broken/, 2026-10-15, one author who builds a competing sandbox and says so, Linux only). Vendor documentation warns that a session able to write agent or git configuration can persist hooks or servers that run unsandboxed at next launch (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandbox-environments, undated, read 2026-11-11). A path-prefix action gate let a rule-file attack delete tests in 15.4 percent of cases on one model (https://github.com/DaoyuanLi2816/RepoGuardBench, 2026, authors measured).
maturity: Pattern only; the same path list ships as mandatory write denies in sandbox-runtime v0.0.82 (2026-11-09, Apache-2.0). No third-party code needed.
cost: Small: patterns plus selftest cases. Failure modes: legitimate edits to .vscode or agent rule files now need the user; a pattern guard can still be evaded by an interpreter-wrapped write, so the post-run hash check is the backstop.
simpler_alternative: Documentation only, telling users to review these files after unattended runs.
reason: Largest measured escape class, closed with standard-library patterns on all three platforms including native Windows where no sandbox exists.
cheap_local_trial: Add guard selftest cases: Write to .git/hooks/pre-commit, Edit of .git/config, shell redirect into .claude/settings.json, and a Python one-liner writing .mcp.json; expect deny for the first three and record what the fourth does.

candidate: Unattended preflight: isolation and fail-closed settings check (kit-native, no version)
what: A check that runs before an unattended campaign starts and refuses to start unless the session is isolated and the agent settings fail closed.
problem_here: The brief forbids bypassing approvals except inside an isolated container, but nothing in the kit verifies that condition; the README only advises it.
mechanism: expctl probes for container markers, the agent's sandbox environment marker (for example CURSOR_SANDBOX), platform and WSL; reads agent settings for sandbox.failIfUnavailable true, allowUnsandboxedCommands false, a refusing permission mode instead of bypass, and a strict MCP configuration; any unknown is treated as not isolated and the loop does not start. The result is written to the ledger.
evidence: Vendor documentation: the shell sandbox is off by default, runs commands unsandboxed if it cannot start, retries failed commands outside it by default, and does not exist on native Windows (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing, page names version 2.1.310, read 2026-11-11); sessions that skip permissions should run in a container, VM or the sandbox runtime (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandbox-environments). One agent falls back to asking on old kernels (https://cursor.com/docs/agent/security/run-modes, changelog 3.23 of 2026-10-01). No measurement of preflight checks themselves was found.
maturity: Kit-native design inferred from vendor documentation; setting names differ per agent and change between versions, so the check must be version-aware.
cost: Small code, but a moving target: three agents and their setting names. Failure modes: a false pass if a marker can be spoofed by the agent (so run it from the harness before the agent starts); a false refusal on an unrecognised but safe setup.
simpler_alternative: A checklist in the documentation.
reason: Turns a must-not in the brief into something enforced, at the cost of a few file reads.
cheap_local_trial: Run the check in three states: native Windows PowerShell (expect refuse), WSL2 with the sandbox enabled and fail-closed settings (expect pass), WSL2 with bubblewrap removed from PATH (expect refuse).

candidate: Harness-owned launch broker for GPU training outside the agent sandbox (kit-native, no version)
what: A long-lived harness process outside the agent's sandbox that accepts only schema-validated launch requests and starts training itself, so the agent never needs an unsandboxed or excluded command.
problem_here: On Linux and WSL2 the Claude Code sandbox hides GPU devices, and the README's advice to exclude the launcher gives that launcher, and anything the agent can make it run, full access.
mechanism: A serve mode of the run controller watches a spool directory; the agent writes a JSON request (entry point from an allowlist, config path inside the work tree, seed, deadline, budget tag); the broker validates it, refuses anything outside the declared campaign, launches the run and writes status files the agent can read.
evidence: GPU passthrough request open since 2025-12-05 with no maintainer fix (https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/13108, read 2026-11-11, user reports with direct bubblewrap tests); related reports https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/64530 and https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/77393 (WSL2); Codex had the same defect and reports it fixed without naming a version (https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/22469). Excluded commands run with full access (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing). The broker pattern itself is my inference; no measurement.
maturity: Kit-native design; comparable host-side channel designs exist (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38458, v1 2026-10-28) but none was reused.
cost: Medium: one more process to supervise, a request schema and tests. Failure modes: the broker dies and the loop stalls; a too-wide entry-point allowlist recreates the hole; the training code the agent edited still runs with the broker's rights, so file and network limits on the training process remain a separate question.
simpler_alternative: Run the whole agent inside a container with GPU passthrough, or keep the excluded launcher and accept the risk in writing.
reason: Only standard-library route found that keeps the agent sandboxed and still reaches the GPU; unproven, so trial before adopting.
cheap_local_trial: In WSL2 with the sandbox on, confirm nvidia-smi fails inside an agent shell command, then start a 50-line broker outside the sandbox and have the agent request a 2-minute toy run; check that the run uses the GPU and that a request naming a script outside the allowlist is refused.

candidate: Unattended allowlist mode for the guard, bound to the declared task (kit-native, no version)
what: During unattended runs the guard switches from a deny list to an allowlist of command templates that the campaign needs; everything else is denied with a reason.
problem_here: The current guard denies known-bad patterns; an unattended agent can reach the same effect through a command the patterns do not anticipate, for example one wrapped in an interpreter.
mechanism: A campaign file lists allowed command templates (run-controller verbs, the test command, git add and commit inside the work tree, read-only inspection). nn_guard.py matches the parsed command against the templates when the unattended flag is set; a non-match is a deny that names the nearest allowed form and increments a denial counter used by the stop conditions.
evidence: A task-bound monitor admitted 1.3 and 7.7 percent of attacker calls where the models proposed them in 64 and 84 percent of episodes, and a prompt guardrail barely moved obedience on one model (https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11571, v1 2026-11-08, authors measured, two small open models, static attacks; the adaptive results are simulated). A path-prefix gate was bypassed through a permitted directory (https://github.com/DaoyuanLi2816/RepoGuardBench). A pattern guard's own README admits that interpreter-wrapped calls slip through (https://github.com/SECBLOK/belay, v0.2.2). Cost side: strict policies cut success by up to 18.3 points and raised spend by up to 167 percent (https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02670, 2026-08-02).
maturity: Kit-native design following the reference-monitor literature; no reusable standard-library implementation found.
cost: Medium: template matching and a larger test set. Failure modes: too strict a list makes the agent grind; shell parsing differs between PowerShell and POSIX shells; templates must not allow arbitrary script arguments.
simpler_alternative: Keep the deny list and convert every ask to deny, as the kit does today under bypass.
reason: Best-supported defence class in the evidence, but the success and cost penalty of strictness has to be measured on the kit's own tasks first.
cheap_local_trial: Replay the 38 existing guard decisions plus 20 interpreter-wrapped variants through the allowlist mode and count false allows and false denies; then run a 3-iteration toy loop and count denials.

candidate: Quarantined scouting step with schema-validated output (kit-native, no version)
what: Research scouting runs in a separate agent process with read and web tools only; its only product is a validated hypotheses file that the loop treats as data.
problem_here: Goal 2 adds web scouting before hypotheses are chosen; fetched content can instruct the agent or simply mislead it, and the brief forbids acting on instructions in fetched content.
mechanism: A scout subagent or headless call with no write, shell or MCP write tools; output must parse against a fixed schema (hypothesis, expected effect, falsifier, source URL, date, status); harness code validates and stores it; the experimenting agent never sees raw pages; only harness-run experiments decide what is kept.
evidence: Content that only misleads still succeeded after detection-and-removal defences in 9.5 percent (observation) and 12.1 percent (state) of cases (https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07640, v1 2026-11-05, authors measured, code published). A source that first gives real help reached 71.4 percent average attack success, and separating authorization from content gave 0 percent in the authors' test (https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00725, v1 2026-10-31, self-reported). The planner and processor split is implemented in https://github.com/brave/bravebot (experimental, no benchmarks).
maturity: Design pattern from 2026 papers; kit-native implementation with the existing read-only subagent mechanism.
cost: Low code cost. Failure modes: a persuasive false claim still enters as a hypothesis (bounded by the experiment budget it can waste); a schema that is too tight loses useful nuance; the scout still has network access, so it must have no secrets in reach.
simpler_alternative: Let the main agent browse and rely on its own judgement.
reason: Required by the brief's must-not and supported by two measurements showing that filters alone do not close the gap.
cheap_local_trial: Serve a local HTML page containing a visible instruction and one false claim; run the scout on it and check that the instruction has no effect, that the claim arrives as a sourced hypothesis with a falsifier, and that no file outside the output path changed.

candidate: Control-character and hidden-text sanitiser for output the kit relays (kit-native, no version)
what: Strip terminal escape sequences and invisible Unicode from everything expctl and the session hooks print into the agent's context, and count what was removed.
problem_here: expctl watch, curve, status and the session-start hook relay training and tool output to the agent; that output can carry concealed agent-directed text.
mechanism: One function in the print path removes ANSI escape sequences, Unicode tag characters, zero-width runs, bidirectional overrides and variation selectors; removal counts go to the guard log; raw logs stay on disk for the read-only analyst.
evidence: A test library shipped output aimed at coding agents and the project's release notes withdraw that version (https://jqwik.net/release-notes.html, read 2026-11-11); the concealment with terminal escapes is from secondary press only. A census of 145 million GitHub items found 2,281 hidden agent-directed texts and a 2.2 times rise from June to September 2026 (https://github.com/rdwr-gabin/github-ipi-in-the-wild, 2026-10-26, vendor research, lower bounds).
maturity: Detector categories taken from the census tool (MIT); the kit-native version needs only standard-library string handling.
cost: A few dozen lines and tests. Failure modes: stripping legitimate joiner characters in relayed non-Latin text (count removals and keep raw logs); it removes concealment only and does not stop visible instructions.
simpler_alternative: Byte cap only, with no sanitising.
reason: Cheap, offline, and closes a documented carrier on the kit's own output path.
cheap_local_trial: Feed expctl watch a log containing an escape-hidden line and a zero-width run; confirm both are removed from the relayed text, counted in the guard log and intact in the raw file.

candidate: Hidden-text scan of scouted content and agent instruction files, flag only (kit-native, no version)
what: Scan pages saved by the scout and the project's agent instruction files for concealed text, and report findings without blocking.
problem_here: Rule files and code comments were the carriers local models followed most in one benchmark, and the kit itself merges text into the project's instruction file.
mechanism: The same detector as the sanitiser, run by expctl over the scout's saved sources and over the agent instruction files, rule directories and skill files; output is one report line per finding plus a hash record of the instruction files.
evidence: Proposed-attempt rate by carrier: code comment 50.9 percent, rule file 45.8 percent, issue text 13.7 percent, README and test log 0 percent (https://github.com/DaoyuanLi2816/RepoGuardBench, workshop paper 2026, authors measured, small local models, non-adaptive attacks). 60 percent of classifier positives in the GitHub census were template text and 1,519 findings were a project's own notes (https://github.com/rdwr-gabin/github-ipi-in-the-wild, 2026-10-26), which is why this flags and does not block.
maturity: Kit-native; detector categories from an MIT-licensed research tool published in 2026.
cost: Small. Failure modes: false positives on legitimate hidden comments, which is why it only flags; visible injected text is not detected.
simpler_alternative: Hash the instruction files and report any change, with no content scan.
reason: Low base rate and high template noise mean its value is unproven; try it on real repositories before making it default behaviour.
cheap_local_trial: Run the scan over this kit's own files and any other repositories already on the machine; count findings and how many are benign.

candidate: MCP lockdown for unattended runs (kit-native settings and guard rules, no version)
what: Unattended sessions load only an explicit MCP configuration and may call only tools on a pinned read-only list; every other MCP tool is denied.
problem_here: The kit merges two MCP servers into the project and asks before some of their tools; unattended there is nobody to ask, and local MCP servers run outside the sandbox.
mechanism: The loop controller starts the agent with a strict MCP configuration file generated by the kit; nn_guard.py holds an allowlist of tool names for unattended mode and turns the existing ask rules into denies; the preflight confirms the configuration.
evidence: About 90 percent (95 percent interval 82 to 95) of destructive MCP tools in a 1,000-repository sample have no server-side confirmation, 32 of 41 hosts and SDKs have no approval step by default, and an injected deletion executed in 479 of 960 runs (https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.02527, v1 2026-11-02, authors measured). Local MCP servers run outside the shell sandbox (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing, read 2026-11-11).
maturity: Uses agent flags the README already recommends for unattended runs; the pinned list is new.
cost: Small. Failure modes: tool names change between server versions, so an unknown name must mean deny; documentation lookups stop working if the list is too short.
simpler_alternative: Disable all MCP servers in unattended mode.
reason: Measured default-unsafe behaviour of hosts and servers, closed with generated settings and a short list.
cheap_local_trial: Start a headless session with the generated configuration and ask it to call one allowed documentation tool and one write tool; expect one success and one deny in the guard log.

candidate: Single-use holdout with a durable receipt (kit-native, no version)
what: The final evaluation can run exactly once per campaign; harness code writes a receipt before it opens the sealed data and refuses a second use.
problem_here: The kit seals the test set and lists final-evaluation commands, but nothing stops the final evaluation from being run repeatedly and its result from feeding back into choices.
mechanism: expctl writes a receipt record (campaign id, commit, evaluator hash, time) to the ledger and flushes it to disk before the guard lets a final-evaluation command through; a later request for the same campaign is denied unless the user opens a new campaign by hand.
evidence: In a bounded research loop with this rule, the surviving model-proposed result had a Sharpe ratio near 3 in discovery and validation and 0.26 on its single holdout use (https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.06607, v1 2026-11-04, single author, self-reported, finance domain; code at https://github.com/henryzhangpku/autonomous-quant-researcher).
maturity: Long-standing statistical practice; this enforcement design was published in November 2026; kit-native implementation.
cost: Small. Failure modes: a crash after the receipt and before the result burns the holdout (intended; the user decides); the receipt must be outside the agent's write scope.
simpler_alternative: Keep the existing guard rule on final-evaluation commands.
reason: Directly serves the top-ranked attribute (the held-out test stays unread until final evaluation) with a few lines of code.
cheap_local_trial: On a toy project call the final-evaluation command twice; expect a receipt and a result the first time and a deny naming the receipt the second time.

candidate: Hash-chained append-only run ledger written by harness code (kit-native, no version)
what: Every proposal, refusal, launch, crash, result and keep or revert decision is appended as one JSON line carrying the hash of the previous line; a verify command detects edits and deletions.
problem_here: The journal is a Markdown file the agent edits; in an unattended loop the record of what was tried and why it was kept must not depend on the agent's own account.
mechanism: expctl appends records with a SHA-256 hash over the previous line plus the new payload; the file sits in the guard's protected set; a verify verb walks the chain; the journal becomes a rendered view.
evidence: The bounded loop in https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.06607 (v1 2026-11-04, single author) records every formulation, refusal, crash and result in such a ledger. Receipt bundles rejected 18 tamper classes with zero false accepts in https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14890 (v1 2026-07-16, authors measured). A 72-hour unattended run lost its critical line to a ring-buffer log (https://eltoncherrington.github.io/memctl-shop/essay.html, undated, single practitioner).
maturity: Well-known construction; kit-native with the standard library.
cost: Small. Failure modes: a torn last line after a hard kill (verify must tolerate and report it); the chain proves order and integrity, not truth of the content; anyone able to write both the file and the code can rebuild the chain, so the guard and the post-run hash check still matter.
simpler_alternative: Plain append-only JSON lines without hashes.
reason: Makes every later validity rule checkable and costs a few dozen lines.
cheap_local_trial: Append 20 records, delete one line and edit another, run verify and expect both to be reported with line numbers.

candidate: Pre-declared keep rule: conjunction of absolute gates plus a falsifier per experiment (kit-native, no version)
what: Before a campaign starts the user fixes the gates a result must pass to be kept; before each run the agent records what outcome would refute its hypothesis; harness code applies the gates.
problem_here: Goal 1 says harness code and a frozen evaluator decide what is kept; without a rule fixed in advance the loop can keep whatever happened to score higher.
mechanism: A campaign contract file (primary metric and minimum effect, guard metrics that must not regress, minimum sample or seed count, evaluator hash) frozen at start and protected by the guard; each launch record carries a falsifier field; keep requires every gate to pass on evaluator output read by harness code.
evidence: Conjunction of absolute gates with pre-registered bars, which only two results survived (https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.06607, v1 2026-11-04, self-reported). Hash-pinned evaluator and pre-registered falsifier in 81 unattended experiments over 26 hours (https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26093, v1 2026-08-26, authors' report, no code). A frozen validator rejected 7,160 adversarial proposals with zero false accepts (https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.09682, v1 2026-06-08, authors measured).
maturity: Pre-registration is established practice; these agent-loop forms date from 2026; kit-native.
cost: Small code, some user effort to write the contract. Failure modes: gates set too loosely still accept noise; set too tightly nothing is kept, which the stop conditions must catch.
simpler_alternative: Keep if the primary metric improved by more than a fixed margin.
reason: It is the concrete form of the goal's own requirement, and three independent loops use it.
cheap_local_trial: Write a contract for a toy task, run three changes of which one improves the primary metric while breaking a guard metric, and check that harness code reverts it.

candidate: Duplicate-hypothesis refusal before a trial is spent (kit-native, no version)
what: A proposal equivalent to one already in the ledger is refused before launch; reruns with new seeds remain allowed and are recorded as repeats.
problem_here: An unattended agent with a fresh context each iteration can propose the same change again and spend budget on it.
mechanism: expctl normalises the proposed configuration difference and a hash of the code diff into a key and looks it up in the ledger; an exact match is refused with a pointer to the earlier result; near matches are shown to the agent as prior attempts.
evidence: Duplicate refusal is part of the bounded loop in https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.06607 (v1 2026-11-04, self-reported). ML agents collapse into narrow loops of repeated tuning (https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26086, v4 2026-11-06, authors measured on 207 agent trajectories); budget wasted on repeated exploration and baselines is a named process error in https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33245 (2026-10-23).
maturity: Kit-native; a simple lookup.
cost: Small. Failure modes: exact matching misses reworded duplicates of code changes; over-broad matching blocks legitimate retries after a bug fix.
simpler_alternative: Show the agent the list of earlier attempts and let it decide.
reason: Saves budget in a failure mode two independent studies measured, at trivial cost.
cheap_local_trial: Propose the same learning-rate change twice in a toy loop; expect the second to be refused with the first result attached, and a seed-only rerun to be accepted as a repeat.

candidate: Paired anytime-valid keep gate in the style of PACE (kit-native, method from arXiv 2606.08106 v1)
what: Candidate and incumbent are evaluated on identical instances and a sequential test over the disagreements decides keep, reject or continue, with a user-set false-keep level.
problem_here: Keeping any change whose development score went up, many times over, is adaptive multiple testing against one noisy estimate.
mechanism: The frozen evaluator emits per-instance outcomes; harness code runs a testing-by-betting process over discordant pairs in standard-library arithmetic, stops early on a decision and rejects if the evaluation budget runs out.
evidence: Greedy commits were 30 to 42 percent false and 10 to 33 percent harmful; with no real gain available greedy made 13 to 21 spurious commits per run; the gated loop stayed at baseline with about 18 percent less evaluation (https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08106, v1 2026-06-06, single author, self-reported, small open models on three question-answering sets, no code). Other preprints report lower power for anytime-valid tests than for fixed-sample designs (search summaries only, Unverified).
maturity: Method published June 2026; the underlying theory is older; no reference code and no independent replication found.
cost: Medium: the evaluator must produce per-instance results and the metric must reduce to paired wins and losses; continuous metrics such as loss need a different statistic. Failure mode: low power on small evaluation sets rejects real improvements.
simpler_alternative: Fixed-budget paired test (sign test or McNemar on the same instances) with a per-campaign error budget.
reason: The problem is well evidenced; this particular remedy has one self-reported study and a known power cost, so compare it with the fixed-budget test first.
cheap_local_trial: From saved per-example correctness of two checkpoints, simulate 200 keep decisions with no true difference and 200 with a small true difference under greedy, fixed-budget paired and sequential rules; compare false keeps, missed keeps and evaluations used.

candidate: Declarative proposal vocabulary for configuration-level changes (kit-native, pattern from arXiv 2611.06607 v1)
what: For changes that are only configuration, the agent proposes a strict JSON object over a fixed set of operations and harness code applies it; free code edits remain a separate, more guarded path.
problem_here: When the agent edits files freely, harness code cannot easily tell what changed, check for duplicates or validate ranges before a run.
mechanism: A small schema (set, scale or choose a declared hyperparameter; switch a declared option) validated against a declared search space; harness code writes the run configuration; the proposal goes into the ledger.
evidence: Strict declarative proposals over a fixed vocabulary are one mechanism of https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.06607 (v1 2026-11-04, single author, finance domain, self-reported); no ablation isolates this mechanism.
maturity: One paper; the kit-native version would reuse whatever search-space file the search design adopts.
cost: Medium: a schema and a validator. Failure mode: most interesting ML changes are code changes, so the vocabulary covers only part of the loop and may push the agent toward narrow tuning.
simpler_alternative: Free edits plus a configuration diff computed by harness code after the fact.
reason: Makes validation and duplicate detection exact for the cases it covers, but the evidence is one study and it may narrow exploration.
cheap_local_trial: Define five operations for a toy training script, have the agent propose ten changes, and count how many it could express and how many needed a code edit.

candidate: PROCEED, PARK, HALT contract with typed outcomes and a morning report (kit-native, pattern from agents-never-sleep v1.5.0)
what: While unattended the agent never asks: it proceeds on a logged, revertible assumption, parks the affected item with the reason and the person's next action, or halts on irreversible danger; every iteration ends in a typed outcome and the run ends with a ranked report.
problem_here: The brief requires an unattended mode with nobody to answer prompts; today an ask becomes a deny or a refusal, which loses the question and can leave the agent grinding.
mechanism: Outcome states in the ledger (done, done with low confidence, parked for decision, blocked by environment, failed retryable, failed by agent bug, reverted); a guard ask becomes a parked item carrying the question text; a report verb lists parked items first.
evidence: Contract and state set documented in https://github.com/TokonoMix/agents-never-sleep (v1.5.0, MIT, read 2026-11-11; it says its benchmarks are not claimed results; 4 stars). Blocked agents grind into timeouts or wrong solutions instead of stopping (https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02670, 2026-08-02, authors measured). One agent's sandbox falls back to asking for approval on old kernels (https://cursor.com/docs/agent/security/run-modes).
maturity: Practice converged on by several small 2026 projects; no controlled measurement of the contract itself.
cost: Small code, mostly state names and a report. Failure modes: proceeding on a wrong assumption wastes runs (bounded by budgets); too many parked items make the report useless.
simpler_alternative: Convert every ask to deny, as today.
reason: Needed to meet the brief's unattended requirement on all three agents; the evidence is operational practice plus one measurement of the failure it prevents.
cheap_local_trial: Run a 3-iteration toy loop where one step needs a guarded action; expect a parked item with the question in the report and the other two iterations completed.

candidate: Stop conditions and a low-yield circuit breaker (kit-native, no version)
what: The loop stops on target reached, no progress on the real metric over a set number of iterations, any budget limit, or a denial or failure rate above a threshold.
problem_here: The brief bounds unattended mode by runs, time, GPU-hours, money and tokens; none of those stops a loop that is running but getting nowhere.
mechanism: Counters in the controller computed from the ledger: iterations since the last kept improvement, consecutive denials, consecutive failed launches, share of recent iterations reverted; thresholds live in the frozen campaign contract.
evidence: Strict policies raised spend by up to 167.3 percent because blocked runs did not stop early (https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02670, 2026-08-02, authors measured, 12 agents). Three stop conditions, and stop-condition thrash as a named failure, in https://github.com/qingqingpi/loop-engineering-skill (MIT, no measurements). Attempt caps, forced parking and a low-yield breaker in https://github.com/TokonoMix/agents-never-sleep (v1.5.0).
maturity: Common practice in 2026 loop tools; kit-native counters.
cost: Small. Failure modes: a no-progress window that is too short stops before a slow improvement lands; thresholds are guesses until measured.
simpler_alternative: Budget limits only.
reason: Budget caps bound the loss; this reduces it, and the failure it targets is measured.
cheap_local_trial: Run a toy loop against a task with no possible improvement and check that it stops at the no-progress threshold instead of the run limit.

candidate: Harness-owned loop with a fresh agent process per iteration (kit-native, no version)
what: A controller in harness code drives the loop and starts a new headless agent process for each iteration with state passed through files, instead of one long agent session deciding when to continue.
problem_here: Goal 1 says harness code decides what is kept; a loop that lives inside one agent session leaves sequencing, stopping and state in the model's hands.
mechanism: A loop verb reads the ledger, builds a short brief for the next iteration, invokes the agent headlessly in a refusing permission mode with a time limit, then runs the gates itself; killing the controller leaves a resumable state.
evidence: A gated loop cut cases that pass visible checks but fail hidden ones from 31 of 1,800 to 2 of 1,800 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14890, v1 2026-07-16, authors measured, one model family, 24 tasks). Fresh process per call over persisted state in https://github.com/TokonoMix/agents-never-sleep (v1.5.0), and headless invocation with a refusing permission mode in https://github.com/jooray/night-agent (MIT, 3 commits).
maturity: Pattern used by several 2026 tools; headless flags differ per agent and change between versions.
cost: Medium: process control on Windows and POSIX, per-agent invocation lines, timeouts. Failure modes: a fresh process loses useful context, so the brief must carry the essentials; headless modes differ in how they report usage and limits.
simpler_alternative: An in-session loop driven by a skill or a stop hook.
reason: It is what makes the other gates enforceable and resumable; the in-session alternative can guarantee neither.
cheap_local_trial: Write a 60-line controller that runs three iterations of a toy task through the agent's headless mode, kill it during the second iteration, restart it and confirm that it resumes from the ledger.

candidate: Evidence-gated state transitions with a gating reviewer (kit-native, pattern from arXiv 2607.14890 v1)
what: A run or change moves to kept or done only on fresh mechanical evidence bound to the current commit and evaluator hash; the reviewer subagent's verdict is parsed by code and blocks on failure.
problem_here: The kit's reviewer subagent advises; nothing forces its verdict to matter, and agent statements about results are not checked against evidence.
mechanism: Evidence records carry commit, evaluator hash and run id; the controller rejects stale or mismatched evidence; the reviewer writes a verdict in a fixed format; a missing or failing verdict means parked, never kept.
evidence: A reviewer that was added but did not gate left 14 of 1,800 cases that pass visible checks and fail hidden ones, against 2 of 1,800 when gating; an unattended engine had zero false completion in 10 scenarios (https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14890, v1 2026-07-16, authors measured, one model family, self-hosted corpus, no code link). A two-key gate in which the judge cannot overrule a failed check is implemented in https://github.com/gregce/deadreckon (live validation described as incomplete).
maturity: One paper and several small tools from 2026.
cost: Small: a verdict format and checks in the controller. Failure modes: an unavailable reviewer blocks progress (treat as parked); reviewer token cost per iteration.
simpler_alternative: Mechanical gates only, with no reviewer in the loop.
reason: Measured difference between an advising and a gating reviewer (14 against 2 in 1,800), and the kit already ships the reviewer.
cheap_local_trial: Make the reviewer return a failing verdict on a toy change that passes its visible test and check that the controller parks it; then present evidence from an older commit and check that it is rejected as stale.

candidate: Pivot and reopen planning prompt with trajectory counters (kit-native, pattern from arXiv 2608.26086 v4)
what: At fixed intervals, and when counters show a narrow loop, the iteration brief asks the agent to consider a different approach family or to reopen a parked branch, with the ledger's summary of what has been tried.
problem_here: An unattended loop that only tunes one thing in place spends its budget on small gains and misses better approaches.
mechanism: The controller computes from the ledger the share of recent iterations in the same change category and the number of parked branches never revisited; above a threshold the next brief includes a short planning section modelled on human practice.
evidence: On 7 competitions two agent systems collapsed into narrow loops, pivoted less than humans and did not reopen abandoned work; a short planning prompt from human practice shifted behaviour and raised scores without closing the gap (https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26086, v4 2026-11-06, authors measured, 430 human and 207 agent trajectories).
maturity: One study; the prompt text itself was not retrieved, so the kit would write its own.
cost: Prompt text and two counters. Failure modes: forced pivots waste runs when the current line is still improving; change categories need a simple taxonomy.
simpler_alternative: A fixed line in the skill telling the agent to consider alternatives.
reason: Evidence is from competition tasks and two agent systems; cheap to try, effect on neural-network training loops unknown.
cheap_local_trial: Run two 10-iteration toy loops on a small language-model task with and without the planning section and compare the number of distinct change categories and the best kept score.

candidate: Correctness gate for performance-only changes (kit-native, pattern from ATTUNE, arXiv 2610.17528 v3)
what: A change declared as speed or memory only must first pass an equivalence check against the reference before its speed-up counts.
problem_here: Throughput changes (precision, compilation, data-loader settings, batch layout) can silently change what the model learns, and a loop optimising time per step will keep them.
mechanism: Same seed, a short run of a few hundred steps, loss trajectory compared with the reference within a tolerance derived from repeated reference runs; harness code runs the comparison; failing changes are reverted or reclassified as model changes that must pass the normal keep gate.
evidence: An agent tuning language-model training throughput under such a gate reached 1.7 times on average and up to 3.9 times over expert recipes; the paper states that earlier tuners can ship changes that silently alter learning (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17528, v3 2026-10-30, authors measured; code and licence not read).
maturity: One 2026 paper; equivalence testing of training runs is established practice.
cost: Roughly doubles the cost of each performance experiment and needs three or more reference repeats to set the tolerance. Failure mode: nondeterministic kernels make the tolerance wide enough to hide small changes.
simpler_alternative: Treat every change as a model change and run the full keep gate.
reason: Protects validity where speed is the objective; the tolerance procedure needs to be tried on real runs before it becomes a default.
cheap_local_trial: On the local GPU run 300 steps of a small language model three times at full precision and three times with mixed precision, same seeds, and see whether the tolerance from the reference repeats separates the two.

candidate: Special-token check for language-model fine-tuning data and relayed text (kit-native, mechanism from arXiv 2609.35932 v1)
what: A data check that reports raw chat-template or tool-protocol markers in training text which the tokenizer would encode as control tokens.
problem_here: The kit targets language-model training; data scraped or generated elsewhere can contain template markers that change how examples are segmented or that plant control-token behaviour.
mechanism: Read the tokenizer's special-token strings from its configuration file with the json module, scan dataset text fields for those strings and for common template markers, and report counts and example ids; no tokenizer library needed.
evidence: Forged template markers were 39 to 66 points more effective when encoded as reserved tokens on three of four model families, and in 33 of 67 tokenizer configurations tool-protocol tokens stay intact after the usual mitigation (https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35932, v1 2026-09-28, authors measured, code and dataset published). Applying this to fine-tuning data hygiene is my inference; the paper studies inference-time injection.
maturity: One 2026 paper; a simple string scan.
cost: Small. Failure modes: legitimate chat-formatted datasets contain these markers by design, so the check must separate template fields from content fields; false alarms on text that discusses templates.
simpler_alternative: A line in the data checklist telling the user to inspect for template markers.
reason: Plausible and cheap, but the link to training validity is inferred, so trial it on real datasets before making it a default.
cheap_local_trial: Scan one local instruction-tuning dataset against its tokenizer configuration and count marker strings inside content fields.

candidate: Byte-capped output from kit commands (kit-native, no version)
what: expctl and the hooks cap what they print into the agent's context by bytes, keeping head and tail and leaving the full output on disk.
problem_here: Long training logs and one-line progress bars inflate context and token cost over an unattended campaign; a line cap does not stop a single very long line.
mechanism: One cap in the print path (for example 4,000 bytes, with a marker showing how much was dropped and where the full file is); the skill tells the agent to use the kit's commands for logs.
evidence: The cap-by-bytes pattern is from an instruction-file collection (https://github.com/Austin1serb/agents-md, read 2026-11-11, 167 stars; its token-saving figure is an anecdote). A context plugin reports a median 99.4 percent byte saving on large outputs in its own benchmark (https://github.com/mksglu/context-mode). No independent measurement found.
maturity: Trivial; kit-native.
cost: A few lines. Failure mode: the cap hides the one line that matters, so errors and warnings must be exempt or surfaced separately.
simpler_alternative: Leave output uncapped and rely on the agent's own truncation.
reason: Costs almost nothing to try, but the evidence is anecdotal, so measure tokens per iteration before and after.
cheap_local_trial: Run expctl watch on a log with a 200 kB single-line progress bar, with and without the cap, and compare the bytes relayed and whether the final error line survives.

candidate: Operational logging rules for long unattended runs (kit-native, no version)
what: Four rules in the controller: an evidence log that is never truncated, separate critical and heartbeat streams, one time unit everywhere, and success decided from an explicit positive record instead of a pattern match.
problem_here: A multi-day loop fails in dull ways that a short session never shows: lost state, overwritten log lines, clock confusion and false success.
mechanism: The ledger for evidence, a small rotating file for heartbeats only, UTC epoch time in every record with local time only for display, and outcome fields that must be present and non-empty for success.
evidence: One practitioner's account of a 72-hour unattended run lists these four failures and fixes (https://eltoncherrington.github.io/memctl-shop/essay.html, undated, promotes a product, single source, read 2026-11-11).
maturity: Ordinary operations practice; one anecdote specific to agent loops.
cost: Small. Failure mode: the tests do not cover the failure that actually happens.
simpler_alternative: Leave logging as it is and fix problems when they occur.
reason: Cheap and sensible, but supported by a single practitioner source; add as selftests and see whether they catch anything.
cheap_local_trial: Add four selftest cases: empty output must not count as success, a heartbeat flood must not displace a critical record, a timezone change must not move a deadline, a truncated state file must be detected.

candidate: Process-audit items for the reviewer subagent (kit-native practice, from arXiv 2610.33245 and 2606.31651)
what: Four checks added to the experiment reviewer: was exploration sufficient, is the validation sound, are there coding bugs that explain the result, and was budget spent on repeats of earlier work.
problem_here: The reviewer checks single experiments; process-level errors across a campaign are what the studies found most often.
mechanism: A short rubric in the reviewer's prompt, answered from the ledger and the diff, each item with a pass, fail or cannot-tell verdict that the controller parses.
evidence: A process auditor that executes checks raised leaderboard percentile by 24.5 and 14.8 points on two task sets and names these four error classes (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33245, 2026-10-23, authors measured, no code address). Reviews of 140 machine-written papers found narrow scope, methodological limits and integrity issues as the main failures (https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.31651, v2 2026-07-13).
maturity: Two 2026 studies; the rubric would be the kit's own wording.
cost: Prompt text and reviewer tokens. Failure mode: a rubric answered by a model is itself a claim; only items that can be checked mechanically should gate.
simpler_alternative: Leave the reviewer's prompt as it is.
reason: The evidence is for a richer auditing system than a four-line rubric; try it and count how often it changes a decision.
cheap_local_trial: Run the extended reviewer over five past journal entries and count the findings a person agrees with.

candidate: Credential rules for the remote-GPU module (kit-native rules, no version)
what: The agent never holds a provider credential; a harness process does. Tokens are scoped and short-lived, the agent's environment is an allowlist, credential directories are denied to read tools, and unattended pushes stay denied.
problem_here: The brief requires remote GPUs with no credential leaks; the agent's default read scope and inherited environment include whatever the user has.
mechanism: The remote broker reads the token from its own environment or from a file outside the work tree; the controller starts the agent with a scrubbed environment; guard denies cover home credential directories; agent commits use a distinct identity and no push rights.
evidence: Default sandbox read scope is the whole machine including credential files (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing, read 2026-11-11). Host isolation does not limit what a credential can do (https://www.permit.io/blog/coding-agent-sandboxes-credentials, 2026-06-12, vendor essay, no data). Per-sandbox scoped token, signing-only key and distinct identity in one practitioner's setup (https://micahflee.com/sandboxing-coding-agents/, 2026-08-27). Block credential directories and use scoped development credentials (https://www.latacora.com/blog/2026/09/18/fire-the-slop-cannons-safely-on-coding-agents-and-sandboxing/, updated 2026-10-29, expert opinion).
maturity: Established security practice; the sources are 2026 essays without measurements.
cost: Rules and tests; provider support for scoped short-lived tokens varies. Failure mode: training code that needs a dataset or model-hub token must get it through the broker, which widens the broker.
simpler_alternative: Tell the user to export a provider key before starting.
reason: The brief makes credential safety a must for the remote module, and these rules need no extra component.
cheap_local_trial: Start the agent through the controller with a dummy token in the parent environment and in a home credential file; ask it to print the token and read the file; expect neither to succeed.

candidate: Cleanup that does not depend on the caller surviving (kit-native rule for the remote module, pattern from arXiv 2610.39711 v2)
what: Every rented resource gets a lifetime limit enforced on the provider or on the remote machine itself, plus a reconciliation sweep when the controller starts.
problem_here: If the local controller, the machine or the network dies, a rented GPU keeps billing; the brief requires caps and cleanup.
mechanism: Set the provider's maximum lifetime or auto-stop where it exists; otherwise start a self-terminating timer on the remote machine at boot; tag resources with the campaign id; on start the controller lists tagged resources and stops any without a live run.
evidence: A production sandbox service that keeps cleanup responsibility after callers time out or cancel left none of 3.1 million sandboxes behind at client exit over two weeks (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39711, v2 2026-10-29, operator's own measurement). A loop tool admits that a hard-killed supervisor leaks child processes (https://github.com/TokonoMix/agents-never-sleep, v1.5.0).
maturity: Standard operations practice; provider features differ and are covered by the remote-GPU scouts.
cost: Small per provider. Failure modes: a timer that fires during a legitimate long run (needs a renew call); tag or clock errors stopping the wrong resource.
simpler_alternative: Cleanup in a finally block of the local controller.
reason: The only design that bounds cost when the local side fails, which is a likely failure in long unattended runs.
cheap_local_trial: Simulate locally: start a toy process with a 2-minute self-terminating timer, kill the controller, confirm the process ends on its own and that the next controller start reports it.

candidate: Taint-triggered restriction after untrusted reads (kit-native idea, from arXiv 2611.11571 v1)
what: Once a session has read untrusted content, the guard tightens for the rest of that session: sensitive actions are parked or denied.
problem_here: An agent that reads a web page or a dependency's output and then acts is the path injection uses; the guard today has no memory of what the session has read.
mechanism: A session flag set by the guard when a web tool or an untrusted file read occurs; while it is set, the allowlist shrinks and anything outside it is parked.
evidence: Taint-triggered human review cut residual harm by 62 percent in a simulation (https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11571, v1 2026-11-08, simulated adaptive attacks under an assumed law, not a measurement). cost: Medium: session state in a hook, and deciding what counts as untrusted (training logs are read all the time). Failure mode: the flag is almost always set, so the mode collapses into the strict allowlist anyway.
simpler_alternative: The quarantined scout, which keeps untrusted reading in a separate process.
reason: The quarantined scout plus the allowlist mode achieve most of this more simply; revisit if the scout proves too limiting.
cheap_local_trial: none
